text.p: Rising waters on Lake Travis in central Texas forced 300 people out of their homes on Tuesday, but elsewhere in the state once-raging rivers fell back within their banks as rains subsided.

Officials said Lake Travis, which is on the Colorado River just northwest of Austin, would reach near record levels by Thursday as water from heavy weekend rains poured in from the surrounding Texas Hill Country.

Ramona Pavlas, spokeswoman for the Texas Division of Emergency Management, people living in low-lying areas along the 70-mile-long (112 km) lake had been told to leave their homes. Many waded through the slowly rising waters with their possessions held above their heads.

The Red Cross said 450 homes were damaged in an 18-county area by the floods, which struck on Sunday throughout central Texas, but Pavlas said no official assessment of the damage could be completed until the water had subsided.
Five people died in the flooding, including four who were swept down rivers while in their cars, and another who died in a weather-related traffic accident.
The worst of weather occurred in Bandera County, 50 miles (80 km) northwest of San Antonio, Texas, where a total of 21 inches of rain fell over the weekend.
Pavlas said 350 people fled their homes on Sunday in the San Antonio area and that 200 of them were still in emergency shelters as of Tuesday. San Antonio is about 80 miles (128 km) south of Austin.

John Williams, a spokesman for the Lower Colorado River Authority, said Lake Travis was expected to reach 706 feet (214 metres) above sea level -- its second highest level ever -- on Thursday, then begin to recede.
